Welcome to your first class.

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

I understand zoom burnout, and don't want you to suffer. I divide my class into five sections when I teach live, and for ten minutes or so, the cohorts (groups of five) rotate through five tasks. Generally:

You will conduct this activities in the breakout rooms where your cohort is assigned. During breakout, if you have a pressing concern or question, you can assign one person in your group who has the technology to keep zoom and wordpress open at the same time to ask a question on the tlk.io chat window on wordpress. If you have a pressing concern, I will jump into your chatroom, or type a response.

Each member of the cohort will have a job:

1. The herder: Make sure that people aren't pulled off-topic, and make sure that everyone is participating, by asking those who may be quieter to directly give their input.

2. The communicator: will make sure that everyone is connected, and in communication with the instructor.

3. The scribe: Keep notes on what people said, and report to the professor

4. The spokesperson: One person to speak for the group at the end of the class.

5. The time keeper. Make sure that time is divided so that everyone has an opportunity to speak.

These jobs will change within the cohort. Of course, those who may not have the technological capability of jumping between windows should not do the communicator job.

The Stations:

Our groups of five will conduct sessions of seven to ten minutes each depending upon the day and activity. After each session, I will ask for thirty seconds of standing and stretching. Students can mute their video if they wish.

Station One (video on):

This will be a social activity, an ice-breaker, a discussion or some assignment designed to get the cohort to become more unified and get to know the members of the group better.

Station Two (video muted):

This will be a homework section, where students can get started on the homework and record any questions they might have regarding the homework. During this time, students can get up, stretch and move around.

Station Three (video on):

Me. I will ask students to unmute the video and I will take the opportunity to answer questions about homework or class in general. I will also ask for input into the structure of the class.

Station Four (video muted):

This will be a short reading, audio lecture or other activity. During this time, students can mute the screen, stand and stretch, and generally move, as long as they complete the reading of the short text.

Station Five (video off):

This will be a group problem-solving task in which students will be asked to do a two-minute presentation at the end of the class, or it could be a video or audio lecture which students will be asked to discuss afterwards.

It might be chaotic at first, but hopefully we will learn and adapt.

Your MGE .

Activity 1: negotiation

Negotiation Exercise:1.Role playing: You are trying to buy a leather jacket from a street trader in a foreign country whose local currency is valued at 50,000 to 1 of yours. You really like the jacket, which is a good fit, well made and style. But you think the trader is asking too much. Can you negotiate an acceptable price for both of you?Buyer: You have a maximum of 750,000 units of local currency and 100 units of your own. You also have your credit cards. Decide what you want to pay and the tactics you will employ making concessions. A similar jacket in your country will cost about 130 units of your currency.Trader: You have sold seven of these jackets to foreigners in the last few days. The lowest price you received was 300,000 units, the best prices 800,000 units. Most foreigners did not even haggle with you. The jacket cost you 200,000 units. You know that you can buy them more cheaply with foreign currency than your own, which is shaky on the exchange market. In fact, 30 units of the Buyer’s currency would buy you another jacket. You are determined however to make a good profit on this deal.

Activity 2: Your MGE

Your group will do a final project. Each person has a part to play. 

Your grade will be determined based upon the individual work you accomplished, but the more the group cooperates, the more likely you are to succeed.

Each group will have the following members. We used these same designations when I did my walkabouts of NJ, and they work really well for the division of labor.

Poison Ivy: Leader, will fill in jobs that are left undone, makes sure everyone knows what they are doing, and are on point.

Ant: Keeps track of meeting times, fills the sheets that outline who was present at each meeting and who did what for the final project.

Wolf: Makes sure that rules are respected, makes sure that there is no plagiarism, and that conflict is resolved in the group (some barking and some validating is required)

Bat: Is in charge of communication. Makes sure that everyone has each other’s contact information and establishes the best possible way for everyone to communicate.

Otter: Handles technical issues, in charge of editing, recording and film work. 

In charge doesn’t mean exclusive. Each task may require cooperation from various people. But the tasks determine whose academic “head will roll” if things aren’t done. The Poison Ivy’s head almost always rolls, but they aren’t the only one.

Here is your first reading:

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

I'm going to give away the entire plot right here at the beginning of the course: We humans have evolved a capacity to interact with a limited number of people (we will get to know Mr. Dunbar). The theorized upper level of people our brain has the capacity to know and have in our circles is 180 (with other theorists claiming that we can truly know up to 230 people).

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

We will talk about the evolutionary reasons for cultural differentiation, and why we need language and culture to exclude "freeriders" from attempting to appropriate our resources, but we also need allies to help secure these resources.

While we may be excluded from a group, that should not surprise or offend us. We can actually admire and adapt aspects of other cultures that we are excluded from, and we can become "sojourners", people accepted as outsiders by other groups.

How will we use this information?

We will also study and attempt to develop ways to move from the status of outsider to insider quickly while reducing cultural shock. This ability to move has deep implications for people who study marketing and publicity, peacemaking, art, religion and even health studies.

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". These are: economics, technology, disaster, belief, family, religion, geography, ideas, education and individuals. We will examine how these engines interact to create and sustain culture.

Along the way, you will:

  1. Learn to write a T-PAD
  2. Study your own heritage
  3. Learn about New Jersey and share your knowledge with the world (creating a display for the Peace Corps display case in The Great Hall, and sending those very NJ items to children somewhere in the world)
  4. Learn about cultural taxonomy and frameworks and how they explain our actions.
  5. Work as a team to create a cultural consulting group that advises an individual on a real-life cultural problem.

I love teaching this course. It's one of my all-time favorites to teach. I hope that this format will be useful to you and that you will surprise yourself with what you accomplish and how it can help you out there in the world.

So let's get started with our goals for today. In today's class, we will get to know each other a little better, we will learn the routine of the class, we will discover what a T-PAD is, and we will cover the syllabus.

Why WordPress?

I chose to use WordPress as our default platform because I believe that it is important that you create work that you can share with future classes and to create a work that you can share with the world. When you spend a great deal of time writing a paper, generally the only people to ever read that paper are you and your professor. I think that definitely influences what you believe and hope in terms of the quality of your work. I teach this course almost every semester, and I hope that by using WordPress, I'm creating a "dynamic textbook" which will allow your contribution to be shared forever. I'm hoping you will create work that should be shared forever.

That being said, you might sometimes want to create a redacted version of your work for public viewing. The way to do that is to create your text, submit it on ecampus as usual, and then delete the information you do not wish to share. Then paste what's left to WordPress.

I also use WordPress because it allows me to embed elements of the entire class in a single webpage. You will see google docs and google forms, for instance, which you can access directly on this site. I hope that doing so will help make this semester easier to navigate.

What will happen each class?

I understand zoom burnout, and don't want you to suffer. I divide my class into five sections when I teach live, and for ten minutes or so, the cohorts (groups of five) rotate through five tasks. I will be assigning permanent cohorts by class. This means you MUST sign in through monmouth.zoom.us . It is an essential time saver and we will go over how to do that.

With these reading TPAD's you'll learn. I will drop the lowest three.

Hello. I'm Professor Cipriani (I identify he/him/his). I want to get you acquainted with the way our Intercultural Communication class will be run.

If, twenty years from now you still remember one thing from this class, I hope it is that you are aware that culture itself evolves from the human instinct to both include and exclude others in order to acquire and distribute resources. This sounds cold, but resources can be wonderful intangibles, the seratonin release we feel, for instance is a resource, new, more efficient ways of doing things can also be a resource.

If, twenty years from now you take away one thing from this class, I hope it is a friend you made among your cohort groups here. The greatest measure of success in college comes not from what you learn, but who you learn from. That should only be 10% me, 40% yourself, and 50% your fellow students.

We will study how a child learns culture and how that knowledge has an enormous impact on how that child remembers and sees the world. We will begin to understand the concept of schema, perception-action loop, habit and custom.

How will we use this information?

We will study intercultural win-win negotiation, and hopefully give you some tools you can use in your everyday life to move towards agreement and consensus.

We will use our knowledge to begin to understand the way resource distribution, and therefore culture itself, is driven and changed by what I call "engines of cultural change". Hello all.

I am hoping that, instead of zooming into class on Wednesday, you all can arrange a watch party for King of Masks. Go somewhere, have breakfast together and hang out. If you do this together as a cohort, I will allow you all to collaborate on the TPAD (you can submit identical versions) and then I will grade them, and if you want to improve your grade, you can re-write those parts on your own. I ask you to collaborate only if you get together as a cohort to watch, no more than one person on facetime, the rest of you all together.

What I would ask you to do is to be honest if you are able to get together and tell me. For my own purposes, I would enjoy a picture of you together somewhere watching (maybe during class time). We will watch the first 30 minutes of the video today, and you will watch the remaining 1 hour and nine minutes on Wednesday, either alone or as a group. This will give you eleven minutes (at least) to collaborate. Again, ONLY if you have met somewhere to watch the video as a cohort, you can all submit identical TPADs.

The TPAD will be due the Saturday the 23rd. In the Paraphrastic section, I would like you to pay close attention to the cultural dimensions presented. Is this a collectivist culture? Is the main character collectivist? What can you say about power distance? By the way, all the "face changing" in the movie is actually happening in real time with no special effects. The art of rapid mask changing you see is real.

The most important part is the affect analysis. At what points are you most uncomfortable? The most moved? Track your emotions throughout the movie. Pause the movie from time to time. It is important understand that the creator of the movie is communicating from the point of view of a social critic or artist talking to people from his own culture.

The terms are the Cultural Dimensions as described by Hofsteade. You can also use other cultural dimensions. Choose five and define them based on examples from the film. I will list the Hofsteade dimensions here. It is good to observe them as if the world in the film were real, but extra points if you can observe what the filmmaker thinks of that cultural perspective. Since your Terms may take up a great deal more of the word count than the paraphrastic, your word count will be based upon using at least 50 words in this terms section. Three of the terms MUST, please, come from a scene more than a half hour into the movie.

Power Distance:

Uncertainty Avoidance:

Individualism/Collectivism:

Masculinity/Femininity:

Long/Short Term Orientation:

Indulgence/Restraint:

If you find these difficult, you might want to look into the cultural dimensions of Kluckhorn. You can use five of those instead, and they may be more relevant to the film.

TERMS

Intercultural Communication

The exchange of information between individuals from different backgrounds of learned behavior.

Culture

A series of behaviors that are invented, not acquired, and passed on through learning within a group.

Verbal Communication

The exchange of information through spoken or written language.

Nonverbal Communication

The exchange of information through non-linguistic means, such as body language, facial expressions, or gestures.

Sender

The individual or entity that initiates a message in the communication process.

Receiver

The individual or entity that interprets and processes the message in the communication process.

Miscommunication

A failure to convey information accurately or understand a message as intended, often due to cultural differences or other factors.

Cultural Context

The background, habits, and perceptions shared by members of a culture that influence how messages are sent and interpreted.

Filtering

The process of separating relevant information (meaning) from irrelevant information (noise) in communication.

Sojourner

An individual who temporarily resides in a different culture and must adapt to its communication norms and practices.

Noise

Anything that interferes with the transmission or understanding of a message. It could be literal background noise, but in this context, it more broadly includes any irrelevant information or distractions that could impede clear communication. Culture teaches us what is noise and what isn't.

We are going to look at Agents of Change. Two major agents of change are technology and crisis. After this video was made, post-covid PISA scores began to plummet in Finland. The cultural freedom that children had to be children meant an early adoption of devices without limitation. Finland now ranks 11th among nations for reading and math. Overall, every nation, except Japan and China have declined. China is now #1, Singapore is #2, and Finland is #7. US is #20. Globally, reading scores declined by fifteen points and math scores by twenty points. The Pandemic accounts for some of this, but the scores had been declining before the Pandemic. The largest difference was cellphone use.

China severely limits and controls use of cellphones among children under the age of 18.

  • Children under 8 are limited to 40 minutes of phone use per day.
  • Those aged 8-16 are allowed 1 hour of screen time daily
  • No one under 18 can to access their screens between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. while using the minor mode.
  1. Additional features:
  • The minor mode automatically closes online applications when time limits are reached.
  • Users receive a reminder to rest after using their device for more than 30 minutes.
Declining PISA Scores Finland, once renowned for its high-achieving students, has experienced a steady decline in its PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) scores since 2007, coinciding with the introduction of smartphones1. The latest PISA study revealed Finland's lowest-ever average scores in math, science, and reading, prompting the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture to describe the situation as "extremely disconcerting"1. Digital Distraction The 2022 PISA data showed that over 80% of Finland's 15-year-olds reported being distracted by digital devices during math class, at least sometimes1. This high level of distraction is strongly associated with lower academic achievement. Excessive Screen Time Finnish teenagers reported spending more than four hours on digital devices during the school day, ranking Finland sixth overall in digital device usage at school according to the 2022 PISA study1. This excessive screen time is likely contributing to the erosion of learning outcomes. Early Smartphone Adoption A particularly concerning trend in Finland is the early age at which children receive smartphones: Most Finnish children receive their first smartphone (or smartwatch) at age 5 or 61. A 2022 survey indicated that virtually all first-graders in Finland owned phones, including phone watches1. This early adoption of smartphones may be exacerbating the "phone-based childhood" phenomenon, which has been linked to sleep loss, addiction, attention problems, and social deprivation1.

You final.

We are going to talk about the final today.

You are going to be assigned a country and a negotiation goal.

First, you have to validate a concern. You have been sent to one of these countries to determine what the concern, or issue is, surrounding what is going on. Use validation techniques, but sensitive to the cultural dimensions to establish what your counterpart wants.

Your job:

  1. Representing one of the players, your first job is to validate the claim of the person you are negotiating with. You need to do that within the context of the culture you are addressing. Use the validation script, but modify it to account for cultural differences.

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Kurdish Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Strong collective identity
  • Family/tribal honor central
  • Shared historical context
  • Community-based understanding

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate Kurdish greetings and honorifics: "Roj baş" (Good day) with proper respect markers

Listen while:

  • Showing deep respect for tribal/family status
  • Maintaining appropriate eye contact
  • Acknowledging group presence if applicable
  • Showing patience with narrative

2. Reflection Phase

"With respect to you and your family..." "If I understand our discussion..."

Mirror while:

  • Including collective context
  • Acknowledging family honor
  • Respecting tribal traditions
  • Maintaining appropriate formality

3. Verification Phase

"Have I honored your meaning correctly?" "Please guide me if I have misunderstood..."

4. Continuation Phase

"Our people have much wisdom to share..." "Please continue if there is more to tell..."

5. Validation Phase

"This understanding comes from our shared experiences..." "One can see how our people's wisdom shows..."

6. Empathy Phase

Collective emphasis: "Our community carries such experiences..." "Many among us would feel deeply about..."

7. Closing Phase

"Thank you for sharing this wisdom..." "May our people continue to support each other..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Honor tribal/family connections
  • Acknowledge collective struggles
  • Respect traditional hierarchies
  • Include community context
  • Reference shared cultural understanding

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Russian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Formal but direct communication
  • Strong respect for hierarchy
  • Less emphasis on positive reframing
  • Professional distance maintained

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin formally using proper name and patronymic: "[Name] [Patronymic], I am ready to listen."

Listen while:

  • Maintaining professional posture
  • Showing attention through direct eye contact
  • Limiting verbal interruptions
  • Respecting hierarchy

2. Reflection Phase

Direct but formal: "If I understand correctly, [Name] [Patronymic]..." "Allow me to reflect what you have shared..."

Mirror while:

  • Maintaining formal language
  • Being direct but respectful
  • Acknowledging position/status
  • Keeping professional distance

3. Verification Phase

Clear but formal checking: "Have I understood your position correctly?" "Please correct any misunderstanding."

4. Continuation Phase

"Would you like to add anything further?" "Please continue if there are additional points."

5. Validation Phase

Direct but respectful: "Your position is logical considering..." "One can understand your conclusion based on..."

6. Empathy Phase

Reserved but acknowledging: "Such a situation would naturally be challenging..." "One can understand the seriousness of this position..."

7. Closing Phase

Professional closing: "Thank you for sharing your perspective." "Your input is valued and understood."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Maintain professional boundaries
  • Respect hierarchical structures
  • Limit excessive emotional expression
  • Focus on practical understanding
  • Acknowledge position/status

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Iranian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Incorporate ta'arof (ritual courtesy)
  • Poetic/indirect communication
  • High context culture
  • Strong emphasis on social harmony

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with formal greetings: "Salaam" (with appropriate honorifics - "Agha" for men, "Khanoom" for women)

Listen while:

  • Showing deference through body language
  • Using appropriate verbal acknowledgments
  • Maintaining respectful eye contact
  • Practicing patience with narrative style

2. Reflection Phase

With extreme courtesy: "If I may be so honored to reflect your precious words..." "With your gracious permission, I understood that..."

Mirror while:

  • Using poetic language when appropriate
  • Maintaining formal address
  • Including social context
  • Acknowledging family honor

3. Verification Phase

Very indirect checking: "I hope I have not misunderstood your valued meaning..." "Please honor me with any corrections..."

4. Continuation Phase

"If you would grace me with any additional thoughts..." "Your wisdom surely has more to teach..."

5. Validation Phase

"Your words carry the wisdom of our traditions..." "One can clearly see how your understanding flows from..."

6. Empathy Phase

Indirect and poetic: "Such situations would move any noble heart..." "The gardens of our hearts are watered by such experiences..."

7. Closing Phase

Extended, formal closing: "I am honored by your trust..." "May your family continue to be blessed..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Never rush ta'arof exchanges
  • Respect complex status hierarchies
  • Include appropriate religious/cultural references
  • Maintain poetic/indirect style
  • Honor family connections

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Syrian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • High context communication style
  • Strong emphasis on face-saving
  • Religious and family honor central
  • Indirect emotional expression

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with "As-salaam-alaikum" and appropriate honorifics "Bismillah" (In the name of God) if appropriate

Listen while:

  • Maintaining modest eye contact (especially across genders)
  • Using appropriate religious acknowledgments
  • Showing deep respect through body language
  • Remaining patient with storytelling style

2. Reflection Phase

"If Allah permits, let me try to understand what you have shared..." OR "With your permission, I have heard that..."

Mirror while:

  • Using "we" language
  • Including family context
  • Referencing appropriate religious/cultural values
  • Maintaining indirect style

3. Verification Phase

Very indirect checking: "Would you help me understand if I have captured your meaning..." "Inshallah, I hope I have understood correctly..."

4. Continuation Phase

"If Allah wills, perhaps there is more to share..." "Your words carry wisdom - please continue if you wish..."

5. Validation Phase

"By Allah's wisdom, what you say carries truth..." "In our tradition, such [references to situation] are understood..."

6. Empathy Phase

Very indirect: "Many in our community would feel deeply about such matters..." "Such situations touch the heart of any family..."

7. Closing Phase

"Alhamdulillah for this sharing..." "May Allah grant wisdom/ease in this matter..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Strict gender protocols - modify script accordingly
  • Heavy emphasis on religious/cultural references
  • Family honor paramount
  • Avoid direct emotional labeling
  • Respect age/status hierarchy

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Turkish Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Use "siz" (formal you) form throughout
  • Maintain appropriate honorifics
  • Include religious references naturally
  • Remember family/collective context

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate greeting: "Merhaba" (or "Selamün aleyküm" if appropriate) Express honor at listening: "It would be my honor to listen to your thoughts on this matter."

Listen attentively while:

  • Maintaining respectful but not overly direct eye contact
  • Using gentle head nods
  • Offering soft verbal acknowledgments ("evet")
  • Showing patience without interruption

2. Reflection Phase

When the speaker pauses, respond: "Sayın [appropriate title], if I may reflect what you have shared..." [using formal language] OR "[Title] Bey/Hanım, with your permission, I understand that..." [for less formal situations]

Mirror content while:

  • Including family/community context
  • Maintaining formal language
  • Acknowledging status differences
  • Using appropriate religious references when natural

3. Verification Phase

Check understanding respectfully: "If I may ask, have I understood your meaning correctly?" OR "Please correct me if I have misunderstood anything you've shared."

4. Continuation Phase

"Would you honor me with any additional thoughts on this matter?" OR "If there is more you would like to share, I am here to listen."

5. Validation Phase

"What you have shared makes complete sense, especially considering [reference to family/community values]..." "I understand how, from your position and experience..."

6. Empathy Phase

Indirect approach: "Such situations naturally bring forth strong feelings in our community..." "Many would feel [emotion] when facing such circumstances..."

"Thank you for honoring me with your trust in sharing this." Include appropriate religious closing if context allows: "Allah kolaylık versin" (May God make it easy)

  • Adjust formality based on age/status differences
  • Increase indirect communication with higher status individuals
  • Include family/community context throughout
  • Use appropriate religious references based on person's religious observance

Negotiation Scenarios Chart for Key players in Syria

Here are the key interests of all players, besides the US and Israel.

First, express a concern across culture. For instance, you are a sojourner into Iranian culture. Use this chart to help, and then each of you conduct a Black Swan-type negotiation.

Now, Russia wants guarantees of safety to their personnel and equipment evacuating Syria.

Key Observations

  1. Competing Interests:
    • Most players (Turkey, Kurds, Syria) have overlapping but conflicting territorial and sovereignty goals, especially in northern Syria.
    • Iran and Russia align in supporting Assad but differ on their ultimate long-term influence.
  2. Potential Areas of Agreement:
    • Stabilization of Syria is a shared goal for all parties, though the definition of "stabilization" varies.
    • Economic incentives (e.g., reconstruction contracts) could be used as leverage for cooperation.
  3. Points of Leverage:
    • Turkey can leverage its control of border zones and refugee management.
    • Russia has influence over both the Syrian government and Turkey.
    • The Kurds have strategic importance as a buffer against extremists and Turkish incursions.

Here are obstacles to asks and offers:

Turkey

  • Obstacle 1: Limiting Pressure on Iranian-Backed Militias
    • Issue: Turkey risks straining its relations with the U.S., which opposes Iranian influence in Syria.
    • Impact: This could jeopardize U.S. military and economic support, including arms deals and NATO coordination.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey might seek to reassure the U.S. by emphasizing its role in countering Russian influence or combatting ISIS.
  • Obstacle 2: Collaboration with Russia
    • Issue: Turkey’s cooperation with Russia, such as on the TurkStream pipeline and northern Syria zones, often conflicts with U.S. and NATO interests.
    • Impact: Strains NATO unity and risks sanctions, such as those imposed after Turkey purchased the Russian S-400 missile system.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey uses its control over NATO’s southern flank and refugee management as leverage.
  • Obstacle 3: Continued Incursions into Kurdish Areas
    • Issue: Aggressive actions against Kurdish forces may alienate both the U.S. (which supports the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF) and Russia (which prefers regional stability).
    • Impact: This could result in diminished influence in broader negotiations or loss of Kurdish cooperation in countering extremism.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey could offer limited recognition of Kurdish cultural rights to de-escalate tensions.

Iran

  • Obstacle 1: Supporting Syrian Government
    • Issue: Iran’s backing of Assad and militias alienates the U.S., Israel, and Turkey, and makes broader regional cooperation difficult.
    • Impact: Increases economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could propose scaling back its forces in exchange for reduced U.S. pressure or security guarantees from Israel.
  • Obstacle 2: Conflict with Turkey
    • Issue: Iranian-backed militias operate near Turkish zones of influence, creating direct tensions.
    • Impact: Hinders Iranian-Turkish collaboration on broader regional issues.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could focus on mediating Kurdish-Turkish tensions to find common ground.
  • Obstacle 3: Expanding Influence
    • Issue: Iran’s growing influence in Syria is a direct threat to Israel, leading to frequent Israeli airstrikes and opposition from Gulf states.
    • Impact: Escalates military risks and complicates relations with Russia, which seeks stability in Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could negotiate with Russia to limit its visibility near Israeli borders.

  • Obstacle 1: Reconciling with Kurds
    • Issue: Offering autonomy to the Kurds could alienate Turkey, which opposes any Kurdish self-governance.
    • Impact: Risks Turkish retaliation or increased military presence in northern Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could frame Kurdish autonomy as limited to cultural or administrative matters.
  • Obstacle 2: Dependence on Iran and Russia
    • Issue: Heavy reliance on Iranian and Russian support limits Assad’s flexibility in negotiations with Turkey, Kurds, and Western powers.
    • Impact: Creates a perception of diminished sovereignty and weakens bargaining power.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could seek balanced deals that allow limited concessions to Western interests while maintaining Russian and Iranian support.
  • Obstacle 3: International Legitimacy
    • Issue: Assad’s regime remains internationally isolated, making it difficult to secure reconstruction funds or recognition.
    • Impact: Limits the government’s ability to stabilize and rebuild the country.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could offer security guarantees to attract Gulf states or Western support.

Kurds

  • Obstacle 1: Balancing Relations with the U.S. and Syrian Government
    • Issue: Cooperation with the U.S. alienates the Syrian government, while aligning with Assad risks losing U.S. protection and aid.
    • Impact: Limits autonomy negotiations and leaves the Kurds vulnerable to Turkish aggression.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could offer anti-terrorism cooperation to both the U.S. and Syria as leverage.
  • Obstacle 2: Dealing with Turkey
    • Issue: Kurdish ambitions for autonomy threaten Turkey’s national security interests.
    • Impact: Invites Turkish military incursions and reduces regional stability.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could agree to demilitarized zones near the Turkish border in exchange for security guarantees.
  • Obstacle 3: Lack of International Recognition
    • Issue: The Kurds lack formal recognition as a political entity, limiting their leverage in negotiations.
    • Impact: Makes it difficult to secure long-term autonomy or aid.
    • Counterbalance: Strengthening alliances with Western powers, particularly the U.S. and EU, for political support.

Russia

  • Obstacle 1: Maintaining Turkey-Russia Relations
    • Issue: Supporting Assad and Kurdish ambitions creates friction with Turkey, a key partner for energy exports.
    • Impact: Risks losing Turkey as a strategic ally and transit country for the TurkStream pipeline.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could mediate Turkish-Kurdish tensions to maintain balanced relations.
  • Obstacle 2: Balancing Iran and Israel
    • Issue: Russia’s partnership with Iran conflicts with its goal of stability in Syria, as Iran’s activities provoke Israeli airstrikes.
    • Impact: Undermines Russian efforts to stabilize Syria and risks alienating Israel.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could limit Iran’s military presence near Israeli borders to appease both Israel and the U.S.
  • Obstacle 3: U.S. Sanctions
    • Issue: Russia’s involvement in Syria contributes to continued U.S. sanctions, limiting economic recovery.
    • Impact: Weakens Russia’s ability to fund its military operations and aid Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could negotiate de-escalation agreements with the U.S. in exchange for reduced sanctions.

This is a great choice for this class.

How Fado and Validation Are Connected:

  1. They know communication is imperfect
    • In Validation, people often misunderstand each other because they interpret words and actions through their own imago.
    • In Fado, the singer expresses deep emotions that words alone cannot fully communicate, and the music fills in those emotional gaps.
    • Both recognize that emotions are often felt rather than logically explained.
  2. They express deep emotions that words may fail to capture
    • Fado conveys saudade—a deep, untranslatable longing—through music, tone, and feeling, not just words.
    • Validation encourages people to express hurt, longing, and needs in a way the reciever can truly hear.
    • In both cases, emotions are not just stated—they are felt and received by the other person.

  • Look for inconsistencies between spoken words and nonverbal behavior. When you’re at the negotiating table, pay attention to how your counterparts speak and act. Remember that their spoken words only account for seven percent of their communication and look for nonverbal cues that contradict their words. It’s also important that you make sure your own nonverbal messages are in line with what you are saying. If your facial expressions are pained and you can’t maintain eye contact, you are communicating your insecurity to your counterpart no matter what you say.
  • Monitor your counterpart’s speaking patterns. We all have one way of telling the truth. If you can identify how your counterpart looks and sounds when they are being honest with you, you’ll be able to detect any deviations from that pattern that may signal a lie. People who are being dishonest tend to use more words and effort than necessary to communicate their point. Use your listening skills to keep an ear out for such verbosity and gain an upper hand.
  • Learn to use different vocal tones. According to the 7-38-55 rule, tone of voice accounts for 38 percent of meaning in communication. Mastering the use of your voice can help you become a better negotiator by improving the delivery of your arguments. In the negotiating room, there are three main tones of voice: Assertive voice is declarative and typically counterproductive.   • Calibrate your own nonverbal communication. Effective communication during a negotiation, conflict management session, or problem-solving sessions requires the ability to calibrate how you communicate. Tap into your listening skills, assess how your counterpart is feeling, and adjust your nonverbal communication in response. This will communicate far more about your reaction than anything you could say to them. When debating the main points in a negotiation, try to alter your demeanor based on the signals you are receiving from your counterpart. Even if your arguments themselves don’t change, changing your nonverbal messaging can be effective.

Use the "calibrated no"

1. “Is now a bad time to talk?”

Replaces: 

  • “Have you got a few minutes to talk?” 
  • “Is now a good time to talk?”

Why use this:

  • This is a great way to practice getting your repetitions in with no-oriented questions and seeing their effectiveness in action.
  • People feel anxious when they sense you are seeking a yes. This relieves your counterpart from wondering what they are getting themselves into if they agree.
  • People feel safe and secure when they say no. This is a great way to learn this concept.

You will only ever get two answers to this question:

  • “Not at all! It’s never a bad time to talk to you. What have you got?” Or something very close to this. When you get a response like this you now have their complete attention—which is what you were after in the first place.)
  • “Yes, it is a bad time. But I can talk with you at (a time they suggest).” Perfect. Again, this is what you were after—their focused attention.

I’m sure you’re wondering: What if they say yes and don’t give you a good time to talk? 

Consider this: Do you want to be on the phone with someone who responds like that? Someone else out there is waiting for you, and this call is keeping you from them. Move on. 

2. “Is it a ridiculous idea … ?”

Replaces:    

  • “Is this a good idea?” 
  • “Would you like to do this?”
  • “Does this look like something that would work for you?”
  • “Would you be willing to … ?”

Why use this: 

  • See above re: No. 1.

This is crucial for solving those obstacles—if they can be solved. If not, you can move on with a clear conscience.

Replaces:

  • “Will you … ?”
  • “Are you in favor of … ?”
  • “Does this look like something that will work for you?”

Why use this:

It replaces the commitment of yes-oriented questions. This is very similar to the second no-oriented question on this list. Both can also be used in combination for clarification of details and commitment to action.   

4. “Have you given up on … ?”

Replaces:   

  • “Do you still want … ?”
  • “Are you still interested in … ?”
  • Any communication to check in with someone who has stopped communicating with you.

This is also the best way to restart communication!

What does the 7-38-55% rule have to do with negotiation?

  • Observe your counterpart’s body language. According to the 7-38-55 rule, 93 percent of meaning is communicated non-verbally. Your tone of voice and body language are much more important than what you’re actually saying. If your counterpart’s body language indicates that they are about to lose their bearings, speak calmly and plainly to soothe them and slow the pace of the negotiation. You should always seek a course of action that encourages the other side to let their guard down. In an effective negotiation, you should try to build a working relationship with your negotiating partner and find ways to defuse tension when possible.
  • Look for inconsistencies between spoken words and nonverbal behavior. When you’re at the negotiating table, pay attention to how your counterparts speak and act. Do the words they’re saying match the way they’re carrying themselves? Look at the people who are not talking—what does their body language signal to you? Remember that their spoken words only account for seven percent of their communication and look for nonverbal cues that contradict their words. It’s also important that you make sure your own nonverbal messages are in line with what you are saying. If your facial expressions are pained and you can’t maintain eye contact, you are communicating your insecurity to your counterpart no matter what you say.
  • Monitor your counterpart’s speaking patterns. We all have one way of telling the truth. If you can identify how your counterpart looks and sounds when they are being honest with you, you’ll be able to detect any deviations from that pattern that may signal a lie. People who are being dishonest tend to use more words and effort than necessary to communicate their point. Use your listening skills to keep an ear out for such verbosity and gain an upper hand.
  • Learn to use different vocal tones. According to the 7-38-55 rule, tone of voice accounts for 38 percent of meaning in communication. Mastering the use of your voice can help you become a better negotiator by improving the delivery of your arguments. In the negotiating room, there are three main tones of voice: Assertive voice is declarative and typically counterproductive. An accommodating voice gently promotes collaboration and should be used most of the time.
  • Calibrate your own nonverbal communication. Effective communication during a negotiation, conflict management session, or problem-solving sessions requires the ability to calibrate how you communicate. Tap into your listening skills, assess how your counterpart is feeling, and adjust your nonverbal communication in response. This will communicate far more about your reaction than anything you could say to them. When debating the main points in a negotiation, try to alter your demeanor based on the signals you are receiving from your counterpart. Even if your arguments themselves don’t change, changing your nonverbal messaging can be effective.

Use the "calibrated no"

1. “Is now a bad time to talk?”

Replaces: 

  • “Have you got a few minutes to talk?” 
  • “Is now a good time to talk?”

Why use this:

  • This is a great way to practice getting your repetitions in with no-oriented questions and seeing their effectiveness in action.
  • People feel anxious when they sense you are seeking a yes. This relieves your counterpart from wondering what they are getting themselves into if they agree.
  • People feel safe and secure when they say no. This is a great way to learn this concept.

You will only ever get two answers to this question:

  • “Not at all! It’s never a bad time to talk to you. What have you got?” Or something very close to this. When you get a response like this you now have their complete attention—which is what you were after in the first place.)
  • “Yes, it is a bad time. But I can talk with you at (a time they suggest).” Perfect. Again, this is what you were after—their focused attention.

I’m sure you’re wondering: What if they say yes and don’t give you a good time to talk? 

Consider this: Do you want to be on the phone with someone who responds like that? Someone else out there is waiting for you, and this call is keeping you from them. Move on. 

2. “Is it a ridiculous idea … ?”

Replaces:    

  • “Is this a good idea?” 
  • “Would you like to do this?”
  • “Does this look like something that would work for you?”
  • “Would you be willing to … ?”

Why use this: 

  • See above re: No. 1. 

This replaces the clarification and micro-commitments of yes-oriented questions.

Also realize that you will often get “No, but …” as a response. The information you get after the “but” is exactly what you need to understand the obstacles standing between you and implementation. This is crucial for solving those obstacles—if they can be solved. If not, you can move on with a clear conscience. 

3. “Are you against … ?”

Replaces: 

  • “Do you agree?” (“Do you disagree?” is also acceptable here as a replacement.)
  • “Will you … ?”
  • “Are you in favor of … ?”
  • “Does this look like something that will work for you?”

Why use this:

It replaces the commitment of yes-oriented questions. This is very similar to the second no-oriented question on this list. Both can also be used in combination for clarification of details and commitment to action.   

4. “Have you given up on … ?”

Replaces:   

  • “Do you still want … ?”
  • “Are you still interested in … ?”
  • Any communication to check in with someone who has stopped communicating with you.

This is also the best way to restart communication!

We are going to look at Agents of Change. Two major agents of change are technology and crisis. After this video was made, post-covid PISA scores began to plummet in Finland. The cultural freedom that children had to be children meant an early adoption of devices without limitation. Finland now ranks 11th among nations for reading and math. Overall, every nation, except Japan and China have declined. China is now #1, Singapore is #2, and Finland is #7. US is #20. Globally, reading scores declined by fifteen points and math scores by twenty points. The Pandemic accounts for some of this, but the scores had been declining before the Pandemic. The largest difference was cellphone use.

China severely limits and controls use of cellphones among children under the age of 18.

  • Children under 8 are limited to 40 minutes of phone use per day.
  • Those aged 8-16 are allowed 1 hour of screen time daily
  • No one under 18 can to access their screens between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. while using the minor mode.
  1. Additional features:
  • The minor mode automatically closes online applications when time limits are reached.
  • Users receive a reminder to rest after using their device for more than 30 minutes.
Declining PISA Scores Finland, once renowned for its high-achieving students, has experienced a steady decline in its PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment) scores since 2007, coinciding with the introduction of smartphones1. The latest PISA study revealed Finland's lowest-ever average scores in math, science, and reading, prompting the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture to describe the situation as "extremely disconcerting"1. Digital Distraction The 2022 PISA data showed that over 80% of Finland's 15-year-olds reported being distracted by digital devices during math class, at least sometimes1. This high level of distraction is strongly associated with lower academic achievement. Excessive Screen Time Finnish teenagers reported spending more than four hours on digital devices during the school day, ranking Finland sixth overall in digital device usage at school according to the 2022 PISA study1. This excessive screen time is likely contributing to the erosion of learning outcomes. Negotiation Scenarios Chart for Key players in Syria, relevant negotiations in December of 2024

Here are the key interests of all players, besides the US and Israel.

First, express a concern across culture. For instance, you are a sojourner into Iranian culture. Use this chart to help, and then each of you conduct a Black Swan-type negotiation.

Now, Russia wants guarantees of safety to their personnel and equipment evacuating Syria.

Key Observations

  1. Competing Interests:
    • Most players (Turkey, Kurds, Syria) have overlapping but conflicting territorial and sovereignty goals, especially in northern Syria.
    • Iran and Russia align in supporting Assad but differ on their ultimate long-term influence.
  2. Potential Areas of Agreement:
    • Stabilization of Syria is a shared goal for all parties, though the definition of "stabilization" varies.
    • Economic incentives (e.g., reconstruction contracts) could be used as leverage for cooperation.
  3. Points of Leverage:
    • Turkey can leverage its control of border zones and refugee management.
    • Russia has influence over both the Syrian government and Turkey.
    • The Kurds have strategic importance as a buffer against extremists and Turkish incursions.

Here are obstacles to asks and offers:

Turkey

  • Obstacle 1: Limiting Pressure on Iranian-Backed Militias
    • Issue: Turkey risks straining its relations with the U.S., which opposes Iranian influence in Syria.
    • Impact: This could jeopardize U.S. military and economic support, including arms deals and NATO coordination.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey might seek to reassure the U.S. by emphasizing its role in countering Russian influence or combatting ISIS.
  • Obstacle 2: Collaboration with Russia
    • Issue: Turkey’s cooperation with Russia, such as on the TurkStream pipeline and northern Syria zones, often conflicts with U.S. and NATO interests.
    • Impact: Strains NATO unity and risks sanctions, such as those imposed after Turkey purchased the Russian S-400 missile system.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey uses its control over NATO’s southern flank and refugee management as leverage.
  • Obstacle 3: Continued Incursions into Kurdish Areas
    • Issue: Aggressive actions against Kurdish forces may alienate both the U.S. (which supports the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF) and Russia (which prefers regional stability).
    • Impact: This could result in diminished influence in broader negotiations or loss of Kurdish cooperation in countering extremism.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey could offer limited recognition of Kurdish cultural rights to de-escalate tensions.

Iran

  • Obstacle 1: Supporting Syrian Government
    • Issue: Iran’s backing of Assad and militias alienates the U.S., Israel, and Turkey, and makes broader regional cooperation difficult.
    • Impact: Increases economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could propose scaling back its forces in exchange for reduced U.S. pressure or security guarantees from Israel.
  • Obstacle 2: Conflict with Turkey
    • Issue: Iranian-backed militias operate near Turkish zones of influence, creating direct tensions.
    • Impact: Hinders Iranian-Turkish collaboration on broader regional issues.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could focus on mediating Kurdish-Turkish tensions to find common ground.
  • Obstacle 3: Expanding Influence
    • Issue: Iran’s growing influence in Syria is a direct threat to Israel, leading to frequent Israeli airstrikes and opposition from Gulf states.
    • Impact: Escalates military risks and complicates relations with Russia, which seeks stability in Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could negotiate with Russia to limit its visibility near Israeli borders.

Syrian Government

  • Obstacle 1: Reconciling with Kurds
    • Issue: Offering autonomy to the Kurds could alienate Turkey, which opposes any Kurdish self-governance.
    • Impact: Risks Turkish retaliation or increased military presence in northern Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could frame Kurdish autonomy as limited to cultural or administrative matters.
  • Obstacle 2: Dependence on Iran and Russia
    • Issue: Heavy reliance on Iranian and Russian support limits Assad’s flexibility in negotiations with Turkey, Kurds, and Western powers.
    • Impact: Creates a perception of diminished sovereignty and weakens bargaining power.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could seek balanced deals that allow limited concessions to Western interests while maintaining Russian and Iranian support.
  • Obstacle 3: International Legitimacy
    • Issue: Assad’s regime remains internationally isolated, making it difficult to secure reconstruction funds or recognition.
    • Impact: Limits the government’s ability to stabilize and rebuild the country.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could offer security guarantees to attract Gulf states or Western support.

Kurds

  • Obstacle 1: Balancing Relations with the U.S. and Syrian Government
    • Issue: Cooperation with the U.S. alienates the Syrian government, while aligning with Assad risks losing U.S. protection and aid.
    • Impact: Limits autonomy negotiations and leaves the Kurds vulnerable to Turkish aggression.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could offer anti-terrorism cooperation to both the U.S. and Syria as leverage.
  • Obstacle 2: Dealing with Turkey
    • Issue: Kurdish ambitions for autonomy threaten Turkey’s national security interests.
    • Impact: Invites Turkish military incursions and reduces regional stability.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could agree to demilitarized zones near the Turkish border in exchange for security guarantees.
  • Obstacle 3: Lack of International Recognition
    • Issue: The Kurds lack formal recognition as a political entity, limiting their leverage in negotiations.
    • Impact: Makes it difficult to secure long-term autonomy or aid.
    • Counterbalance: Strengthening alliances with Western powers, particularly the U.S. and EU, for political support.

Russia

  • Obstacle 1: Maintaining Turkey-Russia Relations
    • Issue: Supporting Assad and Kurdish ambitions creates friction with Turkey, a key partner for energy exports.
    • Impact: Risks losing Turkey as a strategic ally and transit country for the TurkStream pipeline.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could mediate Turkish-Kurdish tensions to maintain balanced relations.
  • Obstacle 2: Balancing Iran and Israel
    • Issue: Russia’s partnership with Iran conflicts with its goal of stability in Syria, as Iran’s activities provoke Israeli airstrikes.
    • Impact: Undermines Russian efforts to stabilize Syria and risks alienating Israel.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could limit Iran’s military presence near Israeli borders to appease both Israel and the U.S.
  • Obstacle 3: U.S. Sanctions
    • Issue: Russia’s involvement in Syria contributes to continued U.S. sanctions, limiting economic recovery.
    • Impact: Weakens Russia’s ability to fund its military operations and aid Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could negotiate de-escalation agreements with the U.S. in exchange for reduced sanctions.

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Kurdish Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Strong collective identity
  • Family/tribal honor central
  • Shared historical context
  • Community-based understanding

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate Kurdish greetings and honorifics: "Roj baş" (Good day) with proper respect markers

Listen while:

  • Showing deep respect for tribal/family status
  • Maintaining appropriate eye contact
  • Acknowledging group presence if applicable
  • Showing patience with narrative

2. Reflection Phase

"With respect to you and your family..." "If I understand our discussion..."

Mirror while:

  • Including collective context
  • Acknowledging family honor
  • Respecting tribal traditions
  • Maintaining appropriate formality

3. Verification Phase

"Have I honored your meaning correctly?" "Please guide me if I have misunderstood..."

4. Continuation Phase

"Our people have much wisdom to share..." "Please continue if there is more to tell..."

5. Validation Phase

"This understanding comes from our shared experiences..." "One can see how our people's wisdom shows..."

6. Empathy Phase

Collective emphasis: "Our community carries such experiences..." "Many among us would feel deeply about..."

7. Closing Phase

"Thank you for sharing this wisdom..." "May our people continue to support each other..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Honor tribal/family connections
  • Acknowledge collective struggles
  • Respect traditional hierarchies
  • Include community context
  • Reference shared cultural understanding

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Russian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Formal but direct communication
  • Strong respect for hierarchy
  • Less emphasis on positive reframing
  • Professional distance maintained

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin formally using proper name and patronymic: "[Name] [Patronymic], I am ready to listen."

Listen while:

  • Maintaining professional posture
  • Showing attention through direct eye contact
  • Limiting verbal interruptions
  • Respecting hierarchy

2. Reflection Phase

Direct but formal: "If I understand correctly, [Name] [Patronymic]..." "Allow me to reflect what you have shared..."

Mirror while:

  • Maintaining formal language
  • Being direct but respectful
  • Acknowledging position/status
  • Keeping professional distance

3. Verification Phase

Clear but formal checking: "Have I understood your position correctly?" "Please correct any misunderstanding."

4. Continuation Phase

"Would you like to add anything further?" "Please continue if there are additional points."

5. Validation Phase

Direct but respectful: "Your position is logical considering..." "One can understand your conclusion based on..."

6. Empathy Phase

Reserved but acknowledging: "Such a situation would naturally be challenging..." "One can understand the seriousness of this position..."

7. Closing Phase

Professional closing: "Thank you for sharing your perspective." "Your input is valued and understood."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Maintain professional boundaries
  • Respect hierarchical structures
  • Limit excessive emotional expression
  • Focus on practical understanding
  • Acknowledge position/status

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Iranian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Incorporate ta'arof (ritual courtesy)
  • Poetic/indirect communication
  • High context culture
  • Strong emphasis on social harmony

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with formal greetings: "Salaam" (with appropriate honorifics - "Agha" for men, "Khanoom" for women)

Listen while:

  • Showing deference through body language
  • Using appropriate verbal acknowledgments
  • Maintaining respectful eye contact
  • Practicing patience with narrative style

2. Reflection Phase

With extreme courtesy: "If I may be so honored to reflect your precious words..." "With your gracious permission, I understood that..."

Mirror while:

  • Using poetic language when appropriate
  • Maintaining formal address
  • Including social context
  • Acknowledging family honor

3. Verification Phase

Very indirect checking: "I hope I have not misunderstood your valued meaning..." "Please honor me with any corrections..."

4. Continuation Phase

"If you would grace me with any additional thoughts..." "Your wisdom surely has more to teach..."

5. Validation Phase

"Your words carry the wisdom of our traditions..." "One can clearly see how your understanding flows from..."

6. Empathy Phase

Indirect and poetic: "Such situations would move any noble heart..." "The gardens of our hearts are watered by such experiences..."

7. Closing Phase

Extended, formal closing: "I am honored by your trust..." "May your family continue to be blessed..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Never rush ta'arof exchanges
  • Respect complex status hierarchies
  • Include appropriate religious/cultural references
  • Maintain poetic/indirect style
  • Honor family connections

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Syrian Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • High context communication style
  • Strong emphasis on face-saving
  • Religious and family honor central
  • Indirect emotional expression

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with "As-salaam-alaikum" and appropriate honorifics "Bismillah" (In the name of God) if appropriate

Listen while:

  • Maintaining modest eye contact (especially across genders)
  • Using appropriate religious acknowledgments
  • Showing deep respect through body language
  • Remaining patient with storytelling style

2. Reflection Phase

"If Allah permits, let me try to understand what you have shared..." OR "With your permission, I have heard that..."

Mirror while:

  • Using "we" language
  • Including family context
  • Referencing appropriate religious/cultural values
  • Maintaining indirect style

3. Verification Phase

Very indirect checking: "Would you help me understand if I have captured your meaning..." "Inshallah, I hope I have understood correctly..."

4. Continuation Phase

"If Allah wills, perhaps there is more to share..." "Your words carry wisdom - please continue if you wish..."

5. Validation Phase

"By Allah's wisdom, what you say carries truth..." "In our tradition, such [references to situation] are understood..."

6. Empathy Phase

Very indirect: "Many in our community would feel deeply about such matters..." "Such situations touch the heart of any family..."

7. Closing Phase

"Alhamdulillah for this sharing..." "May Allah grant wisdom/ease in this matter..."

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Strict gender protocols - modify script accordingly
  • Heavy emphasis on religious/cultural references
  • Family honor paramount
  • Avoid direct emotional labeling
  • Respect age/status hierarchy

Active Listening and Dialogue Script - Turkish Cultural Context

Preliminary Notes

  • Use "siz" (formal you) form throughout
  • Maintain appropriate honorifics
  • Include religious references naturally
  • Remember family/collective context

Script Steps

1. Opening & Listening Phase

Begin with appropriate greeting: "Merhaba" (or "Selamün aleyküm" if appropriate) Express honor at listening: "It would be my honor to listen to your thoughts on this matter."

Listen attentively while:

  • Maintaining respectful but not overly direct eye contact
  • Using gentle head nods
  • Offering soft verbal acknowledgments ("evet")
  • Showing patience without interruption

2. Reflection Phase

When the speaker pauses, respond: "Sayın [appropriate title], if I may reflect what you have shared..." [using formal language] OR "[Title] Bey/Hanım, with your permission, I understand that..." [for less formal situations]

Mirror content while:

  • Including family/community context
  • Maintaining formal language
  • Acknowledging status differences
  • Using appropriate religious references when natural

3. Verification Phase

Check understanding respectfully: "If I may ask, have I understood your meaning correctly?" OR "Please correct me if I have misunderstood anything you've shared."

4. Continuation Phase

"Would you honor me with any additional thoughts on this matter?" OR "If there is more you would like to share, I am here to listen."

5. Validation Phase

"What you have shared makes complete sense, especially considering [reference to family/community values]..." "I understand how, from your position and experience..."

6. Empathy Phase

Indirect approach: "Such situations naturally bring forth strong feelings in our community..." "Many would feel [emotion] when facing such circumstances..."

7. Closing Phase

"Thank you for honoring me with your trust in sharing this." Include appropriate religious closing if context allows: "Allah kolaylık versin" (May God make it easy)

Important Cultural Notes:

  • Adjust formality based on age/status differences
  • Increase indirect communication with higher status individuals
  • Include family/community context throughout
  • Use appropriate religious references based on person's religious observance
  • Show proper respect to eldership/authority

Negotiation Scenarios Chart for Key players in Syria, relevant negotiations in December of 2024

Here are the key interests of all players, besides the US and Israel.

First, express a concern across culture. For instance, you are a sojourner into Iranian culture. Use this chart to help, and then each of you conduct a Black Swan-type negotiation.

Now, Russia wants guarantees of safety to their personnel and equipment evacuating Syria.

Key Observations

  1. Competing Interests:
    • Most players (Turkey, Kurds, Syria) have overlapping but conflicting territorial and sovereignty goals, especially in northern Syria.
    • Iran and Russia align in supporting Assad but differ on their ultimate long-term influence.
  2. Potential Areas of Agreement:
    • Stabilization of Syria is a shared goal for all parties, though the definition of "stabilization" varies.
    • Economic incentives (e.g., reconstruction contracts) could be used as leverage for cooperation.
  3. Points of Leverage:
    • Turkey can leverage its control of border zones and refugee management.
    • Russia has influence over both the Syrian government and Turkey.
    • The Kurds have strategic importance as a buffer against extremists and Turkish incursions.

Here are obstacles to asks and offers:

Turkey

  • Obstacle 1: Limiting Pressure on Iranian-Backed Militias
    • Issue: Turkey risks straining its relations with the U.S., which opposes Iranian influence in Syria.
    • Impact: This could jeopardize U.S. military and economic support, including arms deals and NATO coordination.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey might seek to reassure the U.S. by emphasizing its role in countering Russian influence or combatting ISIS.
  • Obstacle 2: Collaboration with Russia
    • Issue: Turkey’s cooperation with Russia, such as on the TurkStream pipeline and northern Syria zones, often conflicts with U.S. and NATO interests.
    • Impact: Strains NATO unity and risks sanctions, such as those imposed after Turkey purchased the Russian S-400 missile system.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey uses its control over NATO’s southern flank and refugee management as leverage.
  • Obstacle 3: Continued Incursions into Kurdish Areas
    • Issue: Aggressive actions against Kurdish forces may alienate both the U.S. (which supports the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF) and Russia (which prefers regional stability).
    • Impact: This could result in diminished influence in broader negotiations or loss of Kurdish cooperation in countering extremism.
    • Counterbalance: Turkey could offer limited recognition of Kurdish cultural rights to de-escalate tensions.

Iran

  • Obstacle 1: Supporting Syrian Government
    • Issue: Iran’s backing of Assad and militias alienates the U.S., Israel, and Turkey, and makes broader regional cooperation difficult.
    • Impact: Increases economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could propose scaling back its forces in exchange for reduced U.S. pressure or security guarantees from Israel.
  • Obstacle 2: Conflict with Turkey
    • Issue: Iranian-backed militias operate near Turkish zones of influence, creating direct tensions.
    • Impact: Hinders Iranian-Turkish collaboration on broader regional issues.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could focus on mediating Kurdish-Turkish tensions to find common ground.
  • Obstacle 3: Expanding Influence
    • Issue: Iran’s growing influence in Syria is a direct threat to Israel, leading to frequent Israeli airstrikes and opposition from Gulf states.
    • Impact: Escalates military risks and complicates relations with Russia, which seeks stability in Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Iran could negotiate with Russia to limit its visibility near Israeli borders.

Syrian Government

  • Obstacle 1: Reconciling with Kurds
    • Issue: Offering autonomy to the Kurds could alienate Turkey, which opposes any Kurdish self-governance.
    • Impact: Risks Turkish retaliation or increased military presence in northern Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could frame Kurdish autonomy as limited to cultural or administrative matters.
  • Obstacle 2: Dependence on Iran and Russia
    • Issue: Heavy reliance on Iranian and Russian support limits Assad’s flexibility in negotiations with Turkey, Kurds, and Western powers.
    • Impact: Creates a perception of diminished sovereignty and weakens bargaining power.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could seek balanced deals that allow limited concessions to Western interests while maintaining Russian and Iranian support.
  • Obstacle 3: International Legitimacy
    • Issue: Assad’s regime remains internationally isolated, making it difficult to secure reconstruction funds or recognition.
    • Impact: Limits the government’s ability to stabilize and rebuild the country.
    • Counterbalance: Assad could offer security guarantees to attract Gulf states or Western support.

Kurds

  • Obstacle 1: Balancing Relations with the U.S. and Syrian Government
    • Issue: Cooperation with the U.S. alienates the Syrian government, while aligning with Assad risks losing U.S. protection and aid.
    • Impact: Limits autonomy negotiations and leaves the Kurds vulnerable to Turkish aggression.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could offer anti-terrorism cooperation to both the U.S. and Syria as leverage.
  • Obstacle 2: Dealing with Turkey
    • Issue: Kurdish ambitions for autonomy threaten Turkey’s national security interests.
    • Impact: Invites Turkish military incursions and reduces regional stability.
    • Counterbalance: The Kurds could agree to demilitarized zones near the Turkish border in exchange for security guarantees.
  • Obstacle 3: Lack of International Recognition
    • Issue: The Kurds lack formal recognition as a political entity, limiting their leverage in negotiations.
    • Impact: Makes it difficult to secure long-term autonomy or aid.
    • Counterbalance: Strengthening alliances with Western powers, particularly the U.S. and EU, for political support.

Russia

  • Obstacle 1: Maintaining Turkey-Russia Relations
    • Issue: Supporting Assad and Kurdish ambitions creates friction with Turkey, a key partner for energy exports.
    • Impact: Risks losing Turkey as a strategic ally and transit country for the TurkStream pipeline.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could mediate Turkish-Kurdish tensions to maintain balanced relations.
  • Obstacle 2: Balancing Iran and Israel
    • Issue: Russia’s partnership with Iran conflicts with its goal of stability in Syria, as Iran’s activities provoke Israeli airstrikes.
    • Impact: Undermines Russian efforts to stabilize Syria and risks alienating Israel.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could limit Iran’s military presence near Israeli borders to appease both Israel and the U.S.
  • Obstacle 3: U.S. Sanctions
    • Issue: Russia’s involvement in Syria contributes to continued U.S. sanctions, limiting economic recovery.
    • Impact: Weakens Russia’s ability to fund its military operations and aid Syria.
    • Counterbalance: Russia could negotiate de-escalation agreements with the U.S. in exchange for reduced sanctions.
